utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Radman.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your name and surname for the transcript, as well as your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: My name is Jozo Radman; father's name, Franjo. I was born on the 1st of April, 1966 in Travnik. I now live in the village of Zabilje, in the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are married and you have two children; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am married and I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Before the war, in the former Yugoslavia, you did your military service in the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you leave the JNA with a rank?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I did my military service in the JNA in Samobor, and I left with the rank of lance corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now you are a soldier, a member of the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I am a member of the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you hold the rank of captain there, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, perhaps in a few words, in 1991, during all the political unrest in Croatia and then in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you interested in these events?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Of course I was interested, indeed, because it had to do with the Croat people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how did you view these events? Did you realise, and when did you realise, that all of this could lead to a civil war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: First of all, the events that took place in the territory of the Republic of Slovenia, then in the territory of the Republic of Croatia made it obvious to all people that this was spread to Bosnia-Herzegovina, myself included.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was the reason -- or, rather, let me put it this way: In your village of Zabilje, at that time were there any village guards that were organised at the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Already in the spring of 1992, did they function in a rather organised manner by then?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Already from the spring of 1992, every evening in the village there were village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was the purpose of these village guards?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: In the beginning, fear from crime. There were more and more criminals who were engaged in crime. And of course we could not just sit and watch what happened in the municipality of Ravno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Ravno, there was an attack of the JNA, assisted by the Bosnian Serbs, against that village. That was the first war action of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the municipality of Vitez, in the village of Zabilje where you lived, this village is in the immediate vicinity of Sadovace, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, the houses are right next to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Zabilje and Sadovace are the same local community, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, they are. Zabilje and Sadovace are the same local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was the composition of the population of Sadovace like?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: In Sadovace, the population was almost 100 per cent Muslim, except for one Croat house; whereas in Zabilje, the entire population was Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Before this unfortunate war, was there ever any trouble between the two villages?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. We had lots of friends in Sadovace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In 1992, both villages had village guards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, both villages had village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were their mutual relations tense or did they cooperate? And how did they cooperate if they did cooperate?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: During the evening, when the village guards operated, the village guard from Zabilje would go from the communal centre in Zabilje to the communal centre in Sadovace, and the other way around; the village guards from Sadovace would come to the communal centre in Zabilje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Oh, so that is to say that there was contact between the two village guards. Can we assume that they also conveyed information to one another in terms of what they knew?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, by all means. The information mostly amounted to whether an unknown vehicle entered the area on the assumption that it would do something impermissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an example which would demonstrate cooperation between these two village guards?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: On several occasions I personally went to the communal centre in Sadovace. However, I think that the best indicator would be the following: In the summer, a piece of information arrived in our village that the JNA or, rather, the Serbs, right, sent some kind of a sabotage group to Stozerak. Stozerak is a feature above our villages, Zabilje and Sadovace. On that day, together the inhabitants of Zabilje, Sadovace, and the village of Muratovici, which is above Stozerak and which is also a Muslim village, we all went up to Stozerak together. And, indeed, we did not see a thing there, but we did go up there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we say that this is not the only example of such cooperation?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Of course it is not. I already said, and I repeat, that every evening we went from the community centre --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat something if you've said it. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So let us proceed. When did you first receive a call from the municipal headquarters to report in order to prepare for defence against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992 when I went to the front line in Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Before that, that is to say, late in 1991 and until the summer of 1992, you were only active in the village guards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you reported as a volunteer to the HVO headquarters in case there is any need to defend yourselves?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that is to say that in 1991, you already reported as a volunteer in order to set up the defence?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At Galica and Vlasic, just give me yes or no answers to speed things up. In this first action, you were fighting against the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This was a position that would jeopardize the Lasva Valley starting with Novi Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. How much time did you spend in Galica during this first action?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then you returned to the village?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Upon return to your village, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I continued my civilian life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time, were you employed?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, in Vitezit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you continued going to work?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that moment when you returned from that first shift, did you consider yourself to be a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: A civilian. I worked at Vitezit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As for your participation in the village guards, that is what you did of your own free will; right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked you officially, formally, to join the village guards?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During this first action, were you armed?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: At the Vlasic action, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I had an automatic rifle which I borrowed from a colleague who was on the reserve police force, of the civilian police, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have a uniform?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How did you get it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I bought it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness Radman, I'm going to ask you to look at a document here which is part of the evidence we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have Z70.2 given to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness Radman, please read the first page and then look at the second page. On this next page on the top of the page, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is going to fast and the interpreters can't see a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The interpreters can't see the document, and it's not on the ELMO. What is the point? What is the document? I haven't seen it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The document was earlier introduced by the Prosecution and this witness is listed here on exactly on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: According to the defence, this is the document combined by civil authorities where they wanted to record it first volunteers who participated in any manner in the defence of Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the number if you could give it to us again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Z70.2. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what do you want the witness to do with it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like if the witness would recognise his signature on the bottom of the page, why he signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which page is it of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: First page of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Radman, would you look at the first page of the document at the bottom and see if that's your signature?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, signature number two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radman, there are three signatures here and next to every signature, a particular office is mentioned, a particular position. I'm talking about the bottom of the page, please. I'm reading the first name now, Mirko Djotlo it seems to say. It says "coordinator", what would that mean?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Coordinators were persons in the times of the municipal headquarters and they coordinated with municipal headquarters. These were persons, were villages who coordinated with municipal headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You -- your signature is the second one and next to your name it says "commander". Why commander?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Commander because after the municipal headquarters already in April 1993, around the 20th of April, I was appointed commander of the region, of that area, that's why it says commander. It is actually a sequel to the municipal headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this third name which seems to be Perica Djotlo as far as I can see, it says "president of the basic organisation".

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: That is a post that existed before the municipal headquarters. This was organisation through -- in various villages on a party basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that actually these three persons guaranteed that the persons mentioned on that page are precisely those who took part in organised resistance to the aggression?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, let the witness give the evidence, Mr. Kovacic. Don't give the evidence yourself.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You see he simply says, "Yes." It's much more effective if it comes from him. Ask him "What they were doing? Why were they there?" Ask those sort of questions not putting things to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And finally, in relation to this list, another question: On this page, you were registered as a participant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please show your name on this page?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: The name under number three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And your signature is in the right-hand column; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, another question, and then we've taken care of that particular subject. What was your motive? Why were you engaged in these activities related to village guards regardless of the time, 1991, 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Protection of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After this action at Galica, did you engage in other actions in the organisation of the HVO in the struggle against the aggressor, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I went to actions at Turbe, Kamenjas, Slatka Voda, the feature above Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How were you called up for that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Through the municipal headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The system was the same as it was before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, through a coordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it correct that every time you received call-up papers or you were summoned verbally?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Sometimes the coordinator would say that a certain number of men was needed to go to the front line, either Novi Travnik or Turbe, and a certain number of young men would report in keeping with the needs expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was their status?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Civilian. A large number of them returned to the companies where they worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, when was the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade formed to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: In December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In terms of shifts going to the front line, did anything change for you as a fighting man?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, nothing really. Again, the front line was in Slatka Voda/Kamenjas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps now get some kind of permanent assignment? Were you assigned to barracks or were you active somewhere?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: We did not have any barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You went to the sector Mravinjac/Slatka Voda to the north-west of Novi Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did the BH army have its sector there too?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, to our right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Not me. But the men who were on the right, on our right flank, they had contact with the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know when the Vitez Brigade was established?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: In March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did anything change for you specifically with regard to going to the front line?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Well, nothing special. We just get the sector of the Vitez Brigade on the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So a different location on the line, right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, the locality Mravinjac, Kamenjas, Slatka Voda, Viteska and Tomasevic divided a sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: However the enemy remained the same, right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Again, you were activated and deactivated in different shifts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness Radman, in your assessment, when did noticeable tensions appear between the Croats and the Muslims in the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I noticed at the beginning of 1993, when I was going to the front line, that this was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In which situation did you notice this? What was happening?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: We had problems when we were passing Kalinska Street in Novi Travnik. On one occasion our shift members were actually shot at as we were moving towards the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Under whose control was Kalinska Street?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's in Novi Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were there any cases when you could not take the shortest route from Vitez to Novi Travnik, to your positions up there?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes. The last shift was the one when we could not pass through Kalinska, and then we had to go through Stari Travnik, Old Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is to say, you had to take the roundabout road.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, which was in a poor condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness Radman, when were you last in one of the shifts at the defence line?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: About ten days before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The conflict between the Croats and Muslims started when, to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like to introduce one exhibit. I would kindly ask for a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radman, could you please look at this document so that others can see it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have a number? All right. Go on, Mr. Kovacic. We'll get the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's okay. It's Exhibit D100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it will require a 2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "/2," I'm sorry. Yes, D100/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness Radman, I hope you have managed to see this document.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this order, were you sent to this last shift?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I assume that that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How can you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: After the shift, when I was up there at Slatka Vode, yet another shift went up there which happened to be there on the day of the conflict. They happened to be at the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Point 2 of this order stipulates that one platoon from the 2nd Company is being sent to the defence line. What were these companies, actually?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Companies? Those were the people who actually went to the defence line in shifts, that is to say, those people who were rotated in terms of going to the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. We should show you a document so that you could help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the registrar to have document Z653 shown to the witness, please. Could the witness please be shown the version in the Croat language, and could the English version be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please take a look and tell us who signed this document.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: There is no signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What is mentioned here, the officer for SIS of the 1st Battalion, in your opinion, what does the SIS mean? What is this abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: The Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know at the time of the issuing of this document who this was by name and surname?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the first page of this document, item 2, a company is mentioned here and I suppose it means the 2nd Company. Its commander is Slavko Badrov.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In this list of villages, is your village here?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is, the village of Zabilje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The number of men reporting for shifts, does it correspond to the truth?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is those men who went to the front line from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you were one of 29?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does it also mean, this figure, I mean, that men are called up from that list and then they are sent to the front line?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, depending on the need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that all these men are not under arms and active all the time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No. When they come back, they are civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we could move on to your testimony about the earliest days of the conflict in the Lasva Valley. Do you remember where you were and what you were doing on the evening of the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: On the evening of the 15th of April, I was in the social club in Zabilje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Well, next to its building there is a football playground. So we were playing football, and I was up there at the social club.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I was a civilian. I was there as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were you exercising any of your duties as commander of the village guard?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This evening, did you get any information about what might possibly happen the next day?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And who brought this information?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: This information was brought by Mr. Slavko Badrov.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is the commander of that company mentioned in that document.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: He said that he had some information that on the 16th, the Muslims might try to attack somewhere in the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did Slavko Badrov say where he got that information from and how he came by it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, not to me, because after all, there were many of us in this social club.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So what was the instruction he gave you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: To raise the alertness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time -- I'm sorry, I seem to be rushing. At that moment, did he tell you that as a commander, or was it just advice to the village guard?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: It was an information for all of us, to heed to that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time, was Slavko Badrov authorised to activate you as members of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What did you do then when you received that information?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I told the shift which was on duty on village guard at that time to be on the alert and not to patrol between Sadovace and the centre which was in Sadovace. We also let the village guards at Stozerak know to also be on the alert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What is Stozerak? What is it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: It is the dominating feature above our village, right next to the last houses in the village of Brda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From that hill you could observe what was going on, could you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: From the Stozerak feature, one could see from Stari Travnik to Novi Travnik, even to Vitez and even the road to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm going to give a map to the witness. It will be much faster. Not as evidence but just as assistance in his testimony. Sir, you can put one on the ELMO and one in front of the witness. It would be easier for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you now please also, as you answer the questions, point at the localities that you are mentioning. But you have to show it on the ELMO. Is it, then, correct that in the morning you heard gunfire from different directions in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning of the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What kind of information did you begin to get?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Until after 12.00, nothing during the day, except that in the lower part of the municipality of Vitez, a Muslim attack on the municipality had commenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: We reinforced the village guards at Stozerak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you please show us where Stozerak is.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you now point, where is your village?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Here. Yes, right below Stozerak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Stozerak is about what altitude?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Well, it is about 800 metres high.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. How many men did you have now on duty on Stozerak observing?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Fourteen men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about the unit of the army in Sadovace? Did they do anything?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: The unit of the BH army at Sadovace already began to prepare the defence line between Zabilje and Sadovace on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the morning?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you please show us the demarcation. Where was that line? THE COURT REPORTER: Did the witness say 40 or 14?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I mean between villages ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. That line practically separated those two villages. It was a demarcation line between Sadovace and Zabilje?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was a demarcation line between the Sadovace and Zabilje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And on the right-hand side were the Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was the BH army there?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, reinforced by men from Krajina and Karaula. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to interrupt. The interpreters were asking whether the witness said 40 or 14 members of the guard on the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said --

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: At Stozerak there were 14 members of the guards at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned men from Krajina and Karaula. Who are they?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: We termed as men from Krajina all those who had been expelled by the JNA and Serbs from Krajina, and men from Karaula are villagers from the village of Karaula which was in the municipality of Travnik, that is, those who had also been expelled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So they came to the village of Sadovace as refugees and settled there, did they?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: They were provisionally accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that there were both civilians and military among those people?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, there were both civilians and military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And only for the Court, the area of Krajina that you mentioned, what part of Bosnia is it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Up there, Kljuc, Sanski Most, around Banja Luka. Those territories. Around Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Those forces from Sadovace, what did they do next?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: They formed the defence line facing Grbavica; that is, they linked Sadovace and Grbavica and thus cut off the communication between Vitez and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you please show it to us?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What part was now controlled by the army?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: The army controlled the part from Sadovace down the left bank of the Bila river to where it flows into the river Lasva cutting off the communication with Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you show us which part of the Kaonik-Vitez road this main road was controlled by the forces of the army, the one which you showed to us between Sadovace and Grbavica. Which part of the road roughly?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And can any HVO get through?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: They control it between the bridge and the place called Divjak. Nobody can pass through that any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And let us clarify it while we have the map. So, for instance, you in Zabilje, how did you go to Vitez after that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: We went through Mosunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you please show it to us?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: This way and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you took some roundabout roads?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, some roundabout roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that last section of the road does it pass through the SPS factory?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, through the SPS factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And finally, how long did this situation go on?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Until September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us go back to the 18th of April, that is the early days of the conflict. Did you manage to keep -- to hold on to Stozerak?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And who took Stozerak from you and how?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: On the 18th of April of 1993, the forces of the BH army conduct -- launched an attack on the Stozerak feature, and took it that same day. They took Stozerak and some Croat houses in the places Brda, Sucici and Krizici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And how long, in whole, did the BH army hold that feature, at Stozerak?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So until after the Washington Accords?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the front lines in that area around your village did not change more or less; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: In the direction of Sadovace, but on the 19th of May, 1993, the BH army attacked and took the village of Dzotle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And did you suffer any casualties?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Thirteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what were they, military soldiers, civilians, or what?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: They were civilians and military and members of the work platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the time when Stozerak was attacked on the 18th, with the forces you had at your disposal, were you able to put up any resistance?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You did not even try, you mean, to defend Stozerak?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: We did with those 14 men who were up there at Stozerak, but that fell short of the needs in view of the forces which had attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And tell us, when the war broke out on the 16th of April, when did the mobilisation in your village take place?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: After the fall of Stozerak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, was it one, two, three, five days after its fall?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Two days after the fall of Stozerak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Which means sometime on the 20th or 21st of April, is that when you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, around the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that mobilisation, how was it carried out? How and who told you that as of now you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I received the order which said that I had been appointed the commander of the area in the village of Zabilje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And other members of the village guards in the village had also been -- were also notified in some way that as of that moment, they were members of an HVO brigade, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is there any dilemma that as of that moment, you were subject to the discipline and orders of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, as of that date, we were members of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And at that time, who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Slavko Badrov.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And would you know who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that that order defined the sector of your defence?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, the area of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And did you -- were you now assigned to some other area of military operation or the same?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, it remained the territory of the village to be defended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And later on, any time in 1993, did you move to a different position?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, only on the 5th of September, when the attack was launched on Dzotline Kuce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And your group, your unit, was it transferred to other positions or did it always remain on the same positions defending the village?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: We remained on these positions because we did not have enough men to keep any other position except the ones we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And from what you've shown us on the map, is it correct that between the enemy army and your village, the village you lived in, you, the soldiers of the HVO, always held those positions between the army and the village?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was your village always behind you and you always faced the enemy army, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the day when the conflict broke out, did you have any military fortifications in the village or around the village, were they prepared?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were trenches dug later?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Later, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And as far as you can remember, when was it that you dug your first trenches?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: After the fall of Stozerak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And who dug those trenches?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Soldiers themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did any work unit, work platoon come?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes. A work platoon on the 5th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: On the defence line above Zabilje when Dzotline Kuce fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And why did you need that work platoon then?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Because the front line had fallen. A large segment of the defence line was lost. There were very many casualties, wounded and killed, and we were simply not able to fortify our positions then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Why, because of time available or why?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, because of time available and shortage of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness Radman, tell us, please, in 1993, were you visited by officers and, in particular, IPD officers from your battalion or your brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, they did come to visit us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of those visits?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Officers who visited us had the ethical role to put up the morale among the men and also to inform us about duties and obligations both on the defence line and with regard to the civilian population on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness Radman, tell us if on any one occasion, did you conduct any offensive action against a village inhabited by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, in the direction of the defence line held by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever get an order or issue an order to target houses where there were only civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have any prisoners during the war?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were those prisoners civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: They were both civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court, what did you do with the captured civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: We forwarded them to the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I believe they were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that was -- when was it? At what time in the war?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Sometime between the summer of 1993 until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And how did it come to pass that those civilians had been captured by you? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Two women had lost their way and a soldier from Sadovace whom I know personally. There was fog, and he turned up at our defence line. And a judge and a member of the army who were in a car and had got as far as Zabilje, and a member of the civil defence, as he told us. Because up there, there are woods as you can see on the map. They all just turned up there and they were captured and we turned them over to the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that on no occasion -- where -- did you find yourself in a situation where you took some ground and imprisoned the population there?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And all those people simply turned up at the wrong place, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, they had mostly lost their way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have already mentioned it but just to clarify it, you told us that around the 21st or the 22nd, you were appointed the commander of the Sector 1. What did that mean, will you please explain it? What were those sectors, areas, and how did you organise your defence?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: The area denoted the area around the village, the neighbourhood of a village. So sector Zabilje is in the area of Zabilje. Several villages which are linked territorially make up a sector. A commander of an area came from the village concerned. So all along the defence line the commanders of areas came from the villages themselves, and the sector commanders from the territory covered by that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sector, no, your area, did any other unit ever come to help you at some critical points in time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps give us an example, when did they come to help you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: On the 5th of September when Dzotline Kuce fell, then members of Vitezovi came to hold further advance of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So they were invited to reinforce the line which was falling?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, the line was already falling so they came to try to stop the advance so that they would not advance any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And do you remember Vitezovi who came? How many were they, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion, how long did they stay?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: They stayed that day and the next day until a new line was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And at the time when they came, who were they subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Their commander, that is, his deputy because the -- something was killed on entering the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in that area while they were there, were they subordinated to you as the head, as the commander of the area?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you explain the situation to them, the problems dangers localities? Did you give them any such like information so that they could operate that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes. They were assigned to the part of the Defence line which was falling and where we had to stop the advancement of the BH forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So was it during the attack of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, on the 5th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was it who sent the Vitezovi to help you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No. We had only reported to the battalion commander that there was an all-out attack on our area, that the defence line had been broken through, that there were fatalities and those captured, and some of the members had been surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: After you stabilised the line, those reinforcements left.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, the next day after we had stabilised the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness Radman, in your area, the area in which you were the commander during the war, do you remember how many men were killed in your area?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Thirty-six.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the ratio between civilians and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Twenty were soldiers and the rest were civilians and members of the labour platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about the wounded during that time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Somewhere around 130.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Again, civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Military, by and large, but there were also some civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the labour platoon which came to your rescue to dig when Dzotine Kuce fell. Do you know anything about that labour platoon being captured?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the conflict, you were wounded.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, in June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was this a serious injury or was it a less serious injury?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I was shot through my left arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay on sick-leave?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I was treated in the Nova Bila hospital. Because of the full capacity of the hospital, then I was sent home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay at home?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: A few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then you were sent back to the front line.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you resume the same position which you held before your wounding?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was still in the post of the area commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one additional question. Witness Radman, was there any religious structure in your village or in the village of Sadovace?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: There was a mejtef.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it damaged during the war?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, we could not visually ascertain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you, either during the time when you were part of the village guard or later, attempt to damage it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you have had any reason to do so?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness Radman, I want to thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No questions from Mr. Kordic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you just help me with some preliminary matters. First of all, this document Z70.2, can we have that again, please. I'd like your explanation of this document, if you can help us. In your own words, tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: After the end of the war, the stories started being circulated about the property, that is, the property that was inherited by the BiH. Our task in local areas was to list the persons who were part of the resistance, from the outbreak of hostilities until the end, and who were part of the organised resistance. Now, why are there three signatures here? The president of the basic branch --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you short to save time. That's helpful, what you've told us already. We see that the document is headed: "HDZ for the period 1991 to 1992." The significance of that, please?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: "HDZ for the period 1991 to 1992" means the people who joined the organised resistance against the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then we see, of course, that your name is shown as joining up in September of 1991. We also just see that although you've managed to get most names to sign, there were some you didn't get signed. Is that because they were dead or because you couldn't find them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: At the time when we were compiling the list, certain persons were not at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. But what it shows, does it, is that the political party, the HDZ, was regarded as the body organising the military resistance to what was happening? Would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The political party, the HDZ, is the body organising the military resistance; is that right? From what you've already told us.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, at first, and the organised resistance --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You signed this document, as you've told us, at the foot of the first page, or page number 2 but it's the first page, in your capacity as a military commander.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because, for practical purposes, the local political and local military organisations were one and the same thing?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, they were not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, just explain, if you can, please, how you're signing, as it were, a political record, a record of political involvement in the military defence, how you're signing that as a military person? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: In order to have continuity in terms of the involvement of people who were involved in the organised resistance, starting with the president of the principal branch who was there from the establishment of the municipal staffs, this is why his signature is there. And then when a municipal staff is established, the coordinator who was there, he also signs in order to provide continuity. From March 1993, when the Vitez Brigade was established, it is signed by the local area commander just so that full continuity would be established that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does this summarise it: that military resistance was started by the political party and then handed over to the military?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Not military resistance. Organised resistance. But you can't say that it was military resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, as you will know from the structures of the HVO and from Herceg-Bosna, it was the political parties which established the HVO, and the HVO had a military component; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: The HVO itself was a military component.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another matter of background detail from your experience in the army: When the JNA attacked Slovenia, they passed through Croatia as they had to, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: The JNA did stay in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to attack Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I don't know their exact movements, but they did have barracks in Slovenia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Croatia didn't impede the JNA army by blowing up bridges or things of that sort, did it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I don't know much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just have a look at the map that's been used by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm pretty sure, although I haven't been given the map, that the map is identical to our own -- it's identical in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. part, I think, to our map 2271. It's also got the continuation sheet on the left-hand side. I'm pretty sure it's the identical map. It may be that for definition purposes our 2271 will be easier to read. It's that bit of it there, really. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to take your own map back for a purpose in due course, but if you would just lay that one on the ELMO for the time being. I want to understand the geography. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A little bit further to the north. That's it there. Down a bit. A bit further down, a bit further down. That's fine. Thank you very much. So just to orientate the Chamber, if you could possibly come back a bit, in the technical room, so that we can see a little bit more of the map and, in particular, so that we can see Vitez itself, which is just out of view. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you go out of Vitez, through Stari Vitez, you come first to Mosunj, and having passed -- well, you come to Divjak and then Mosunj, and there are two roads up to your village, aren't there? You could go through Divjak or you could go further and take a larger road. Can we come back a bit, get a bit more of the map into the picture, please? Just a little bit more. Zoom out, I think that's the phrase. Thank you very much. So we can see that there are the two roads up to your village: one through Divjak, and then go on a little bit further and there's a main road, is that right, or a more major road?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will remember, and this is to clarify something, that of course your village up there on the northwest of Vitez is immediately in the opposite direction to the village or community of Kruscica, which is presently just off the map to the south. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, we've had some evidence - Witness AS, for the Court's assistance - about a body of soldiers called the Scorpions or the Alfa Force. Now, it happens that the evidence is in a slightly confused state because it refers to both Zabilje and Kruscica which are, of course, contradictory positions. Can you help us, please, with whether the Scorpions or Alfa Force in 1992 had a headquarters in the area of one of those roads leading to Zabilje?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you're telling us, I think, that village guards in some way were different from the Vitez Brigade or the Viteska Brigade; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Village guards were not part of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, nevertheless, you, on several occasions, went off to the front line as a member of the Viteska Brigade, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes. After the establishment of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about before that? Unless I misunderstood your evidence, didn't you go off to the front line earlier than that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I went to the front line after I was called by the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. For which unit or for what group of soldiers did you go to the front line on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: As a member coming from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was able to give you a command that you should go to the front lines at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: The municipal staff sent out these summons, I guess, through a coordinator. They asked that a number of men from our village be sent to the front line against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but who in your local community had the power to order you to do that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Nobody could order me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you went to the front lines, under whose command were you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: When we were at the front line, we were under the command of the shift commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. The shift commander, what unit was he in, the Viteska Brigade or the Tomasevic Brigade or what?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: He was from the shift -- from the village shift, his village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You mean his village at the front line or his village where?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Several of us went from our village, that is, from the surrounding villages to the front line. So of those of us who were there from that group of villages, one was made the commander of that shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well who made you a commander? I'm trying to -- you have been a military man. You've been in the JNA. I'm trying to work out what the command structure was on these occasions when you went to the front line in 1992. Can you explain it to us?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Through coordinators who coordinated things with the municipal staff, these shifts were organised and sent to the front line, and these coordinators then would designate someone. If we wanted to do so, they would designate one of us to lead these men to -- in that shift to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The municipal staff is the municipal staff of Vitez so that this is effectively the Vitez Brigade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Not the Vitez Brigade. The municipal staff of Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when do you think you were first sent to the front lines in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Leaping ahead just to check something, you were injured, I think, in Brda, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So it wasn't July?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Summer of 1993, June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I believe it was June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because if we look at an exhibit, 1463.4, coming your way. The English perhaps over the map on the ELMO, thank you very much. This is a document apparently dated it looks like 1994 in the original, and it's a confirmation that you, I think that's you born in 1966, were wounded on the 22nd of July in Brda in conflict with the Muslims. It says you received minor bodily injuries in the area of the left elbow while performing combat assignment by order of his superior officer. So that appears to be you, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are two things about this, first of all, you see it says quite specifically, that you are a member of the HVO Vitez Brigade since the 8th of April, 1992 and until the 30th of May of 1994. It's quite clear about that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: As a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Not the Vitez Brigade. HVO was established on 8th April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this is signed by Mario Cerkez. Do you remember his signing this document for you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't remember, not exactly when he signed it. And we had no opportunities to go to Mr. Cerkez, the officials who were in personnel went to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But isn't the reality very simply this: That whatever title you may now give to it, you were, when you went to the front lines, effectively working for the group of soldiers that came to be known as the Vitez Brigade or the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No. I went as a member of my village, and it was all under the municipal staff. The Vitez Brigade was formed later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last question on this topic is this: On your own account, was it the same organisation that was sending you to the front line as was coordinating the activities of village guards, as you describe them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No. No. We went to the front line as needed, as sent by the municipal staff. The village guards were independent. They were not under the influence of the municipal staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may come back to that, I may not. Do you accept that the municipal HVO for Vitez was first under the command of Marijan Skopljak and then under the command of Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Marijan Skopljak was the head of the municipal staff. After the establishment of the Vitez Brigade, Mario Cerkez was appointed the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see again we've heard from a witness, same witness, AS, that in the summer of 1992 there were indeed many units of the HVO stationed in and around Vitez. However we are describing village guards and so on, can you help us with your military experience? Were there indeed many units of the HVO stationed around Vitez in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some units of the HVO stationed around Vitez in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992, there were no units in and around Vitez at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Moving on to 1993, do you remember an incident in your area or village where some HVO soldiers were disarmed, eight, I think of them, in number, and there was eventually negotiations about the restoration of their weapons between Sefkija Dzidic and Pasko Ljubicic? Do you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, see or have any experience of BiH soldiers going to the front lines in the period 1992 and perhaps early 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: To the front line against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it the case, and this is page 8.400 in the transcript, is it the case that such soldiers, BiH soldiers were, from time to time, disarmed by the HVO in your area on the way to those front lines?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, a little bit more about one or two of the documents that you've referred to today. Can you have another look, please, at Z653? The English on the ELMO, please, thank you very much. I want your explanation, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the older translation. The Chamber will recall from yesterday's hearings that the present translation has a different title and it's "List of personnel from the 1st Battalion per village of '?' deployment or origin."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radman, you've got the original there in front of you. When we look at, for example, your village under the 2nd Company under the command of Slavko Badrov, what do you say is meant by the reference to the 29 soldiers here?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I am referring to the men who were rotating on duty in Kamenjas and Turbe; in other words, who were going there at certain intervals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So these are not village guards or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: These men were members of the village guards as necessary, but when there was a need to send them to the front line, they formed a shift and went to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in what way were these 29 distinguishable from any other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. village guard participants from the village of Zabilje?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: They were not distinguishable from the village guards in Zabilje except that they were part of the shift that was sent to the line of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that made them members of the 2nd Company under the command of Slavko Badrov whereas all the other village guards, as you would describe them, would have no company commander; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: These 29 would have been under the command of Slavko Badrov, but only those who would be part of the shift who would go to the line of defence and they would be there if the shift commander, who would be Slavko Badrov, they would be under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But there's absolutely no doubt as to these 29 that they were members of the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No. They were members of the village guards. A number of members of the village guards was part of the shift that went to the line of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But were you a member of the Viteska Brigade at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were not engaged in any military activities at all at this time on the 14th of April?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, except for the village guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This may be a convenient moment, it's entirely for the Chamber, but I just want to conclude this. You see I'm going to suggest to you that this document does show, for example, in Zabilje, 29 people, look at the heading of the document, "Viteska Brigade, 1st Battalion Vitez," and I'm going to suggest that this does show that 29 members of the Viteska Brigade in Zabilje in the same way as, and if you turn your attention to the previous entry, in the same way as there would be 12 members of the Viteska Brigade in the village of Santici. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Twenty-nine members of the village guard who were sent to the line of defence. When they were at the line of defence as part of that shift, their commander would have been Slavko Badrov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll adjourn now. Mr. Radman, would you please remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about your evidence. Don't let anybody speak to you about it, and it includes members of the Defence team. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful to our usher who has very helpfully substituted the revised --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to our usher who has helpfully substituted the revised translation for the earlier one of document 653.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Radman, before I part from this document which we were looking at before the short break, this is a document that was actually introduced by Blaskic in the course of his Defence in his trial. What would you say to his description of this document being a composition of the battalion of which the mentioned officer in each case was the commander? What do you say to that description of this document?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I do not see the composition of the battalion here. "Zabilje, 29." I see 29 members of the village guard from Zabilje who go to the defence line in shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you say to the suggestion that, although they were trying to create a proper brigade at the time, they had to rely on units of village composition - one village, one unit - to go to make up a brigade? What do you say to that? Again, coming from Blaskic himself.

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: In the villages at that time, there were no established units yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: See, I'm going to suggest to you that you're trying to understate the professional reality of the Viteska Brigade at the time of which you're speaking. Things were actually very well organised, and what we've got here is a document showing how well organised things were; isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. The organisation in Zabilje, the organisation of the units started only on the 20th of April when, by way of an order, I was appointed commander of this region. That is when the unit was first established.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to recap, trying to understand your use of terminology, do you accept that between April and November of 1992, there was the municipal headquarters of the HVO in Vitez that was running things?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: From April until December. In December, there was the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to the precise dates if it's necessary. But the municipal headquarters of the HVO was under the control of Cerkez; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: No, under the command of Mr. Marijan Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then we come to the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade from November or, you would say, December of 1992 to February of 1993. Do you accept that Cerkez was the deputy commander or commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what Mr. Cerkez did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't know? This is a very small area --

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- we're talking about. Who do you say was in charge of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, please?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: I don't know. There are a lot of levels above -- I mean, I went to shifts and I knew who the commander of the shift was at the time. And then further up, up above, these higher levels, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You certainly accept that Cerkez was in charge of the Viteska Brigade once it was formally formed, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO RADMAN
utterances.text: Yes, in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
